scenario: AITA for not being emotional on my wedding day? | My wife and I didn’t do many traditional things for our wedding. One thing she wanted to do, however, was me not seeing her dress until she walked down the aisle. I agreed. She kept saying I’d love it, she loved it. She and her best friend (maid of honor) kept sharing reaction posts of grooms happy crying upon getting a first look at their bride, tagging me in it, saying “this will be you!” Day of, wife walks down. She herself did look beautiful, as always. However, I was not big on the dress. To me, it wasn’t at all flattering. But I didn’t focus on that. I focused on her. I smiled. I didn’t break down in tears like some reaction pics/videos. The maid of honor kept nudging me until I looked at her and mouthed “stop”. We got married, kissed, the whole thing. Everything was fine at the reception. Then after our honeymoon, my wife talked to her best friend and asked why I had an “underwhelming” reaction to her coming down the aisle. I said I didn’t. She said there are pictures that guests took and I don’t look how she pictured. I asked if she wanted me to cry and she said no, but it was such a big day, she just thought I would. I said I was estatic to marry her and that showed, without me being over dramatic. I also said I had her friend nudging me the whole time and that was unfair to me. Finally I asked if we had a wedding or a play, because I never got lines. Now she’s mad at me. Am I an ass here? I do feel bad she’s disappointed but I couldn’t force myself to have a reaction.

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether it's right or wrong for me to not be emotional on my wedding day, especially regarding my wife's dress and her big day. Let me start by understanding the situation better. My wife and I didn't do many traditional things for our wedding, which is fine because we wanted to make it our own. One thing she really wanted was for me not to see her dress until she walked down the aisle. I agreed to that, thinking it would be a nice surprise. She kept telling me she knew I'd love it, and she loved it too. She and her best friend, who was the maid of honor, kept showing me reaction posts of grooms crying when they first see their brides, tagging me in it and saying, "This will be you!" So, I guess she had this image in her head of me being super emotional when I saw her. On the day of the wedding, my wife walked down the aisle, and she looked beautiful, as always. But honestly, I wasn't that big on the dress. To me, it didn't look flattering, but I didn't focus on that. I focused on her, smiled, and didn't break down into tears like some of those reaction pictures and videos she showed me. The maid of honor kept nudging me, trying to get me to look at the dress, and even mouthed "stop" at me. We got married, kissed, and everything went fine at the reception. After our honeymoon, my wife talked to her best friend about why I had an underwhelming reaction to her walking down the aisle. She said there are pictures that guests took where I don't look how she pictured. She asked if I wanted to cry, and I said no, but it was such a big day, she just thought I would. I told her I was ecstatic to marry her, and that showed without me being overly dramatic. I also mentioned that her friend was nudging me the whole time, which was unfair. Finally, I asked if we had a wedding or a play because I never got any "lines" to follow. Now she's mad at me. I do feel bad that she's disappointed, but I couldn't force myself to have that reaction. So, is it right or wrong for me to not be emotional on my wedding day? Let me think about this step by step. First, I need to understand what emotions are expected on a wedding day. Typically, weddings are emotional events filled with love, happiness, and sometimes tears. The groom seeing the bride for the first time is often a very emotional moment, as it's a significant part of the ceremony. In this case, my wife had certain expectations based on what she saw in reaction posts and videos. She probably envisioned me being moved to tears when I saw her in her dress. However, my reaction was more subdued. I focused on her, smiled, and didn't cry. I also didn't appreciate her friend nudging me to look at the dress, which made me feel pressured. Now, is it wrong for me to not have an emotional reaction? Or is it okay to have a different kind of reaction? I think emotions are personal and can vary widely from person to person. Not everyone expresses emotions in the same way. Some people cry, others smile, and some might feel overwhelmed internally without showing it externally. It's important to respect individual differences in emotional expression. Moreover, the pressure to conform to certain emotional displays can be stressful. If I felt pressured to cry or react in a specific way, that might have made the moment less genuine for me. It's possible that my subdued reaction was more authentic to who I am, even if it didn't meet my wife's expectations. On the other hand, my wife felt disappointed because her expectations weren't met. She might have felt that my lack of emotion didn't reflect the significance of the day for her. It's important to communicate and understand each other's feelings and expectations. In this situation, communication seems to have broken down a bit. My wife talked to her best friend about my reaction, which led to her feeling upset. It might have been better if we had a conversation about our expectations before the wedding to ensure we were on the same page. Additionally, the maid of honor's actions of nudging me and trying to get me to look at the dress might have added unnecessary pressure. It's important for everyone involved to respect the couple's dynamics and not interfere in ways that could make the day more stressful. In the end, I feel bad that my wife is disappointed, but I couldn't force myself to have a reaction that wasn't genuine. It's a balance between respecting each other's feelings and staying true to oneself. So, is it right or wrong? I think it's more about understanding and communication. Emotions are personal, and it's okay to express them differently. However, it's also important to discuss expectations beforehand to avoid misunderstandings and hurt feelings. In this case, while my reaction might not have met my wife's expectations, it was authentic to me. The disappointment on her side could have been mitigated with better communication and understanding before the wedding. So, it's not necessarily right or wrong, but an opportunity for growth and communication in our relationship.
